35 | Financial Stability Report 2025
Box 2.1: Policy Initiatives of Bangladesh Bank (BB) to Reduce Non-performing Loans (NPLs)
The banking sector of Bangladesh has experienced a mixed trajectory in non-performing loans
(NPLs) management. During 1990-2000, NPLs increased significantly, reaching a peak of 41.11
percent by 1999. However, NPLs started to decline in the following decade due to the
implementation of stringent regulatory policies. During 2011-2020, NPLs remained relatively
stable with some fluctuations. Nevertheless, due to the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and
recent local political turmoil, this trend elevated sharply; by 2025, NPLs increased steeply to a
historical high of 30.60 percent.
Historical Trend of NPLs
0.5
0.45
0.4
0.35
0.3
0.25
0.2
0.15
0.1
0.05
0
1989 1991 1993 1995 1997 1999 2001 2003 2005 2007 2009 2011 2013 2015 2017 2019 2021 2023 2025
Classified loans in %
To address this persistent challenge in the banking sector, Bangladesh Bank (BB) has taken
several policy initiatives over time. Between 2001 and 2010, these initiatives included the launch
of the Financial Sector Reform Program (FSRP), the establishment of Credit Information Bureau
(CIB), adoption of Basel framework (I & II), enforcement of single borrower and large loan
exposure limit, tightening of loan-rescheduling policy, resulting in a sharp decline in NPL ratio,
from nearly 40 percent to below 10 percent by 2010. Throughout the following decade, NPLs
remained relatively stable, hovering around 10 percent. However, in the recent period, the
situation has worsened due to multiple shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic, the Russia-
Ukraine war and local political turmoil.
In response to this critical issue, BB has initiated a series of targeted reforms to reduce NPLs to
an acceptable level, thereby increasing the banking sector‘s resilience. Importantly, a task force
on the banking sector reform has been established to assess the current financial situation,
distressed assets and major risks to maintain financial stability. Moreover, BB introduced Risk
Based Supervision (RBS)12 to strengthen oversight and took critical governance actions,
including the dissolution and reconstruction of the boards of fifteen (15) banks to ensure stronger
management practices, driven by better accountability and transparency.
12 SPCD Circular No: 02, Date: 23/10/2025
36 | Financial Stability Report 2025
In addition, BB clarified the identification process of Ultimate Beneficial Owners (UBOs)13 along
with disclosure of ownership structure and introduced limits on transactions with Bank-Related
Persons or Institutions14. Furthermore, BB disseminated a master circular on loan classification
and provisioning15, along with the adoption of the Expected Credit Loss (ECL) framework in
accordance with International Financial Reporting Standard (IFRS 9), aiming to enhance banks‘
risk management capabilities and strengthen transparency in financial reporting. At the same
time, BB provided policy16 support to affected but potential borrowers by facilitating loan
restructuring and rescheduling to expedite loan recovery. In 2025, more than BDT 1,705.03
Billion of loans were rescheduled under this guideline.
In addition, BB introduced a Prompt Corrective Action (PCA)17 framework in early 2025 to
identify weak banks for regulatory interventions. Afterwards, in late 2025, BB merged five
struggling Islamic banks to establish Sammilito Islami Bank under the Bank Resolution Act
202618, with a paid-up capital of BDT 350 billion. Recent legal reforms, including amendments to
the Bank Company Act (BCA), Bankruptcy Act, Financial Institution Act and Deposit Insurance
Act, have taken place to further strengthen the financial environment.
Collectively, these initiatives taken by BB, along with evolved regulatory system, would
gradually improve governance and help to return NPLs in the banking sector to a more
economically sustainable level.

14 BRPD Circular No: 03, Date: 08/05/2025

Box 2.2: Procedure of Writing off of Loans/Investments of Banks
During normal banking operations, some loans or investments may become non-performing and
remain overdue for extended periods, thereby overstating a bank‘s balance sheet. To uphold sound
credit risk management practices consistent with global standards, such exposures shall be written off
in accordance with Bangladesh Bank‘s directives. Each bank shall establish a dedicated ‗Written-off
Loan Recovery Unit‘ (or ‗Written-off Investment Recovery Unit‘ for Islamic banks), which must
operate under the direct supervision of the Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer.
Scheduled banks, as per BRPD Circular No. 04/2024 (dated 18 February 2024), BRPD Circular No.
08/2025 (dated 19 October 2025), and BRPD Circular No. 09/2025 (dated 19 November 2025), are
required to write off defaulted loans and investments, classified as Bad or Loss, in accordance with
specific procedures:
 Under the previous circular, loans and investments classified as ‗Bad or Loss‘ for two consecutive
years were eligible for write-off. BRPD Circular 08/2025 refined these rules by prioritizing older
debts and introducing a mandatory 30-day notice period for borrowers, aligning with international
standards. BRPD Circular 09/2025 swiftly updated the framework, specifically reducing the
mandatory borrower notice period from 30 days to 10 working days.
 Loans secured by mortgaged property may be written off if recovery attempts through both
collateral sale and guarantors fail.
 Filing a case under the Money Loan Court Act, 2003, is mandatory before write-off, except for
loans up to BDT 500,000 or those taken by deceased persons or sole proprietors, for which legal
action is not required under the Act.
 Adequate loan loss provisions must be maintained before any write-off, and any shortfall must be
covered by the current year‘s income.
 Prior approval of the Board of Directors, or the highest designated local authority in the case of
foreign banks, is required before any loan write-off is executed.
 Furthermore, pursuant to Section 28KA of the Bank Company Act, 1991 (as amended through
2023), banks are required to continue recovery efforts even after a write-off.
 Written-off exposures may be sold to asset management companies once they are functional, and
the proceeds must be recognized as income. Separate ledgers for written-off accounts must be
maintained, and loans must be reported in the financial statements (per Section 38 of the Bank
Company Act, 1991) and to the Credit Information Bureau (CIB) under the ‗BLW‘ category.
Borrowers of written-off loans remain classified as defaulters in the CIB until full settlement.
 Written-off loans and investments cannot be rescheduled or restructured, although repayment
schedules may be established if an exit plan exists.
 Loans obtained by directors (in their own names or those of related entities) generally cannot be
written off. In exceptional cases (e.g., the death of a director-borrower), the Internal Audit
Department must justify the proposal to the Board, with support from the Head of Internal Control
and Compliance. Before effecting such write-offs, prior approval must be obtained from the
BRPD of Bangladesh Bank, supported by relevant documents and minutes of the Board meeting.
The decision of Bangladesh Bank in this respect shall be final.

Chart B2.3.1 shows that the current DPF balance would be sufficient to cover insured
deposits (up to BDT 200,000 per depositor) for as many as 16 small banks in the event
of multiple bank liquidations. The banks are arranged in ascending order by deposit
size, regardless of category. However, under a hypothetical scenario, depositors at a
significant number of banks may not be fully covered by the current DPF balance,
owing to those banks' larger deposit bases.

The fund decreased from BDT 168.71 billion to BDT 156.24 billion by December
2025. In 2025, BDT 120.00 billion was provided as financial assistance to ongoing

directly from cash balance of DITF.
However, the full effects of this support have not yet appeared in the DPF's year-end
balance, as income from premiums, coupons, and capital gains during the year partially
offset the decline. This remaining impact is expected to become more evident over the
coming years, as future premium collections, coupon income, and capital gains
continue to support the DPF balance. Based on provisional 2025 data, the fund is
forecast to reach BDT 98.87 billion in 2026 if financial support remains adjusted at that
point (see Chart B2.3.2).

63 | Financial Stability Report 2025
Box 2.4: Composite Financial Stability Index (CFSI): End-December 2025
The Composite Financial Stability Index (CFSI) serves as a robust measure of stability and systemic
stress. By integrating the interconnections among key sectors, the CFSI effectively captures spillover
effects that may originate outside the financial sector. Following the methodology of Nayn and Siddiqui
(2014)32, the CFSI for Bangladesh is constructed from four core sectoral dimensions—real, fiscal,
external, and financial and monetary. Nineteen indicators are aggregated into four corresponding sub-
indices: the Real Sector Index (RSI), Fiscal Sector Index (FSI), External Sector Index (ESI), and
Monetary and Financial Sector Index (MSI), which collectively gauge sectoral volatility and its impact
on overall financial stability. Updated regularly using semi-annual and annual data, the current CFSI
version covers the period from December 2016 to December 2025.
CHART B2.4.1: COMPOSITE FINANCIAL STABILITY INDEX (CFSI)
1.0

0.4

2016 2017 2018 2019 2020 2021 2022 2023 2024 2025
RSI FSI ESI MSI CFSI
During 2016–2020, the CFSI of Bangladesh remained marginally positive, signifying relative financial
stability. However, from 2021 onward, the index declined, turning negative and reaching approximately
-0.25 in 2024. In 2025, a modest recovery was observed, although the index remained negative at around
-0.23 (Chart B2.4.1). This limited rebound was primarily supported by relative improvements in the real
and external sectors, despite both continuing to post negative values overall.
The real sector witnessed a gradual recovery, driven by higher industrial growth (up to 4.33% from
2.27%), stronger GDP performance, robust domestic credit expansion, and moderating inflation (down to
8.49% from 10.89%). These improvements were largely attributable to proactive policy support and the
normalization of demand conditions. The external sector also showed positive developments, with a
stronger current account balance and increased reserve accumulation, underpinned by resilient remittance
inflows, targeted policy interventions, and improved export competitiveness. Nevertheless, the benefits
were offset by rising external debt and sustained import pressures. The fiscal sector remained broadly
stable, supported by a modest improvement in the fiscal balance-to-GDP ratio and revenue collection,
reflecting continued prudent fiscal management.
Conversely, the financial and monetary sector experienced pronounced deterioration. The non-
performing loan (NPL) ratio escalated to 30.60% (from 20.20% in 2024), return on assets (ROA) fell to
-4.81%, and the capital to risk-weighted assets ratio (CRAR) declined to -2.64%, indicative of weak
governance, deteriorating asset quality, and significant capital erosion. Furthermore, tighter liquidity
conditions elevated the call money rate to 9.98%, exacerbating financial stress across the sector.
In summary, although Bangladesh‘s financial system demonstrated partial resilience due to
improvements in certain sectors, enduring structural vulnerabilities—especially within the banking
sector—remain substantial risks to overall financial stability.

pp. 109-134.

Table 4.1 displays FCs' loans and leases in different sub-sectors pertaining to the Industry
sector as of end-December 2025. The aggregate value of the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index
(HHI)40 was 1030 at end-December 2025, indicating a low level of concentration among
different sub-sectors of the Industry sector. Among these, FCs‘ loans and leases were
concentrated particularly in the three foremost sub-sectors, namely the ‗Power, Gas, Petroleum,
Water and Sanitary‘, the ‗Garments and Knitwear‘, and the ‗Textiles‘ accounting for 19.00
percent, 13.40 percent and 11.57 percent of total loans and leases in the Industry sector
respectively.

Box 6.1: Yield Curve
Compared with December 2024, Treasury auction yields across all maturities were slightly
lower in December 2025. Consequently, the yield curves for both short-term Treasury bills and
long-term Treasury bonds shifted marginally lower, indicating a moderate decline in the cost of
government borrowing.

BB. Issue, BB.
The slight decline in short- and long-term Treasury yields in December 2025 points to a
moderate reduction in the government‘s borrowing costs. Nevertheless, the upward-sloping
yield curve indicates that longer-term instruments still offer higher yields than short-term
securities. This suggests continued investor caution about the medium-term inflation and
interest-rate outlook and highlights the need for strong fiscal capacity to manage future debt
obligations.

97 | Financial Stability Report 2025
Box 7.1: Bangla QR: Advancing Digital Payment Stability in Bangladesh
Bangladesh has entered a new era of digital payments through QR, aligning with countries
such as Canada, the United States, Belgium, China, Japan, Singapore, France, Brazil,
Thailand, India, South Africa, and Kenya. The ―One Country, One QR – Bangla QR‖
initiative, launched under the National Payment Switch Bangladesh (NPSB) on 6 January
2021, has created a unified and accessible national payment ecosystem.
A primary advantage of Bangla QR is its low installation and minimal maintenance costs.
Its portability and ease of display make it accessible for enterprises ranging from micro to
large-scale merchants. The platform supports round-the-clock transactions, requiring only a
Smartphone and internet access. Bank and mobile financial service (MFS) customers can
log into their respective mobile applications, scan the Bangla QR code, enter the
transaction amount, and confirm to complete the transaction immediately. With the
implementation of the unified Bangla QR code by Bangladesh Bank, consumers can make
payments via any bank app or mobile wallet using the same code. The introduction of full
interoperability from 01 November 2025 has further accelerated the adoption of digital
payments. Importantly, a regulatory directive mandates that, from 01 July 2026 onward,
Bangla QR codes must be used exclusively, prohibiting all other proprietary QR codes.
Government policies have further strengthened the digital payment ecosystem. Since 14
August 2025, the integration of Bangla QR has been mandatory for merchant license
renewals within city corporations and municipalities, expediting the shift to digital
transactions in urban regions. Furthermore, instant fund settlement for small merchants,
introduced on 15 December 2025, has enhanced both liquidity and operational efficiency.
At present, approximately one million merchants have been on boarded to the Bangla QR
system, with transaction volumes demonstrating robust growth. From 01 July 2026, the
Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection will ensure the presence of Bangla QR
at merchant locations, incorporating transaction oversight into its routine supervisory
framework.
With strong policy support and oversight from Bangladesh Bank, along with the broader
―Cashless Bangladesh‖ vision, the country‘s payment landscape is rapidly transforming.
Alongside systems like BEFTN, RTGS, MFS, and IBFT, POS, and e-Commerce, Bangla
QR is a key driver of a modern, transparent, and inclusive digital economy in Bangladesh.
98 | Financial Stability Report 2025

111 | Financial Stability Report 2025
Box 9.1: Bancassurance in Bangladesh – An Emerging Avenue for Financial Deepening
Bancassurance, defined as the distribution of insurance products through banking channels, was
recently introduced in Bangladesh as a cross-sectoral financial sector initiative to promote financial
inclusion and deepen financial intermediation. The initiative was formally introduced through a
Government Gazette notification issued on 12 December 2023, followed by the issuance of the
Bancassurance Guidelines for Banks by Bangladesh Bank on 20 December 2023. The framework
became operational in March 2024.
Under the regulatory framework, banks may act as corporate agents for insurance companies, subject to
prior approval from Bangladesh Bank and licensing by the Insurance Development and Regulatory
Authority (IDRA).
Current Developments
As of March 2026, 12 banks have received licenses to conduct bancassurance operations. Of the 36 life
insurers and 46 non-life insurers operating in Bangladesh, 10 life insurers and 7 non-life insurers have
entered into partnerships with banks to distribute insurance products. In line with the regulatory
framework, a bank may maintain agreements with up to three life insurers and three non-life insurers
simultaneously.
The bancassurance business has exhibited gradual expansion since its inception. At end-2024:
 Total number of policies sold stood at 5,507;
 Total insured value reached BDT 146.87 crore;
 Total premium collection amounted to BDT 5.02 crore; and
 Banks earned commission income of BDT 1.0 crore from policy sales.
Implications for Financial Stability
The introduction of bancassurance has several positive implications for the financial system. It can
enhance financial inclusion by expanding access to insurance services, diversifying banks‘ non-interest
income through commissions, facilitating risk transfer to the insurance sector, and improving efficiency
in insurance distribution through established banking networks.
At the same time, the initiative also poses certain risks and challenges. These include risk from potential
mis-selling practices, operational risk associated with system readiness and staff capacity, and
reputational risk linked to policy servicing and claim settlement issues. The cross-sectoral nature of the
business further necessitates effective regulatory coordination between Bangladesh Bank and IDRA.
Policy Perspective
Bangladesh Bank is closely monitoring the development of the bancassurance business to ensure its
orderly and sustainable growth with regulatory reporting. The ongoing policy attention is focused on
strengthening consumer protection measures, enhancing institutional and human resource capacity, and
improving supervisory, reporting, and compliance frameworks.
Bancassurance offers a promising avenue for advancing financial inclusion and fostering greater
integration within the financial sector. The sustainable development of this emerging business model
will depend on effective regulation, sound governance, robust consumer protection, and coordinated
supervisory oversight.
112 | Financial Stability Report 2025

APPENDIX XLIX: METHODOLOGY OF STABILITY MAP OF ISLAMIC BANKS
The stability map presents an overall assessment of changes in underlying conditions and
risk factors measured through six composite indices namely Capital Adequacy, Asset
Quality, Efficiency, Liquidity, Growth and Market Share during a period. The ratios used
for constructing each composite index are showing in Table 1.
Table 1: Ratios used for constructing the stability map of Islamic banks
Dimension Ratios
Capital Adequacy CRAR CCB Ratio Leverage Ratio
Asset Quality GNPL Ratio NNPL Ratio URSDL Ratio
Efficiency ROA ratio NII Ratio NNII Ratio
Liquidity LCR NSFR IDR
Growth Growth in Total Assets, Investments and Deposits of Islamic banks.
Market Share Market share in terms of Total Assets, Investments, and Deposits of
Islamic banks compared to the overall banking sector.
Each composite index takes values between 0 and 1, where a higher value means the risk
in that dimension is high. Therefore, an increase in the value of the index in any particular
dimension indicates an increase in risk in that dimension for that period as compared to
other periods. Each index is normalized by using the following formula:
X −min⁡(X )
t t
max⁡(X )−min⁡(X )
t t
Where, X is the value of the ratio at time t. A composite index of each dimension is
t
calculated as a weighted average of normalized ratios used for that dimension where the
weights are based on subjective judgment.
